Monocle of Clarity: Unique Equipment
Cost: NA Artist: Margaret Organ-Kean

Messages.Author: Joe Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3euvqi$i...@feedback.eng.umd.edu>,
Judith Cookson Grunberger <jcoo...@Glue.umd.edu> wrote:
>Ouch! Be careful with this one. My friends and I pretty much play on a
>fair basis. If someone asks you a yes or no question, we will usually
>answer it if it doesn't damage our chances of losing the game. But I
>have an example of how the Monocle can be screwed.
>
>We were down to a three player game. I had just torpored my prey's
>Brujah Justicar with Roreca Quaid (heheheh), and my predator said "You
>know, I wouldn't object if you diablerized Don Cruez." I thought that a
>skill card wouldn't hurt any, so I said, "Do you *promise* to vote
>against a bloodhunt when my prey calls one." He promised. Swore up and
>down. Vowed on his mother's name. So when I diablerized Don Cruez, and
>my prey called a bloodhunt, he indeed voted against the bloodhunt.
>However, one of his *vampires* voted for the bloodhunt with a Dread Gaze
>or Surprise Influence or something, and that pushed it over. Bleh. I
>almost strangled him.

Your opponent also broke two separate rules in doing this. Since
Methuselahs do not get votes just for being in the game, the votes
from vampires are often the only votes a Methuselah has, and they
count as both the vampire voting and the Methuselah voting. So
right there he broke his promise. The second rule he broke is that
since the bloodhunt vote is not an action, no action modifiers or
reaction cards can be played during that vote, so Dread Gaze or
Surprise Influence are illegal to play during the bloodhunt.

You should be mad. He didn't play fair...

Messages.Author: The Bomb
Messages.Body:
In article <3erc51$h...@columba.udac.uu.se> t93...@phekda.tdb.uu.se (Jacob Jonsson) writes:

> This is just another abuse to the Monocle of Clarity.

> Suppose I ask a paradoxquestion
> (like "Will you answer no to this question?")
> what happens?

> Since it can't be answered truthfully but still has
> a y/n answer, does the game hang or what?

> /Jacob "Ban the Monocle" Jonsson

You know, this whole Ban the Monocle string smacks of the worst kind of Rules
Lawyering I've ever heard. There is no need to ban the Monocle if one uses
common sense when interpreting how it should be used. The Monocle says the
owner must ask a "Yes" or "No" question so the owner can't ask things like
"What cards do you have in your hand?." Clearly, this is intended to limit
the power of the Monocle, not give the owner the ability to lead the target
down a road of damning Yes and No answers.

Note also that the Monocle says that the target must answer truthfully, not
that the target must answer specifically "Yes" or "No". And IMO, the truthful
answer to the question "Will you answer "Yes" to my next question" is "I don't
know because I haven't heard the question yet."

I mean, if you want to be really ridiculous and interpret any incorrect,
non-yes or no answer as a declaration of forfeiture by the target when the
target can't possibly know the answer to your stupid question, you could grab
up a bunch of bloodstones in your hand and ask the target, "Am I holding 13
stones? Yes or no?"

Thanks,

The Bomb

Messages.Author: Brent Ross
Messages.Body:
In article <tidleman.8...@sj.unisys.com>,
The Bomb <tidl...@sj.unisys.com> wrote:
// Note also that the Monocle says that the target must answer truthfully, not
// that the target must answer specifically "Yes" or "No". And IMO, the
// truthful answer to the question "Will you answer "Yes" to my next question"
// is "I don't know because I haven't heard the question yet."

Ok, by this logic the only reasonable answer to any monacle question is
"Perhaps". For starters it allows me to be totally truthful in
all cases (I cannot "know" that anything will be true or false,
I can only "precieve" that which seems true or false, even more so about
future events). Secondly, it totally invalidates your use of the card on me
(thus begining the strategically superior answer). Quite clearly not only
the question is bound to yes or no, but the answer has to be as well, else the
card is worthless.

You could remove meta-questions (ie. questions about questions), which
would fix some of the problems this card has (it's far too broad
and extremely unbalancing and shows that WotC has some pretty bad
play testers (as well as proof readers... terrible number of goofs
in Jyhad)). Problem is you can still Catch-22 other players with
"Have you stopped beating your wife yet?" type questions. My
favourite one of these is "Whenever a vampire attempts to bleed
you, will you attempt to block?". If you answer "No" you can
never attempt to block a bleed. If you answer "Yes" you must
always attempt to block any bleed (which is fine when I'm playing
a Brujah deck).

Messages.Author: Stephen E Mynhier
Messages.Body:
All of the debate concerning Monocle has begun to grate me somewhat. I feel
that the power of the monocle is to read the future, not CONTROL the future.
It is somewhat of a crystal ball for vampires. I can certainly understand
people wanting to play to win (I will reasily admit that I do myself) but
we are all playing a game, and it should be approached as such. It's
almost like someone playing a Vampire LARP and then lying about their skills
to everyone. What's the point?

Sorry, just had to vent...
Stephen
